clinicalPearls: Caused by a specific in-frame GAG deletion in TOR1A (encoding torsinA), inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with markedly reduced penetrance (only around a third of carriers develop symptoms)
Most common cause of early-onset isolated (primary) generalised dystonia, with higher frequency in the Ashkenazi Jewish population
Typically begins in childhood or adolescence in a limb, often a leg or foot, and tends to spread to become generalised while sparing the cranial and cervical regions in many patients
It is an isolated dystonia, meaning there is no cognitive decline, ataxia, or other neurological deficit, and imaging is structurally normal
A levodopa trial is important to exclude dopa-responsive dystonia, which can look identical at onset but is dramatically treatable
Symptomatic options include oral anticholinergic and other centrally acting agents and botulinum toxin for focal problems
Deep brain stimulation of the internal globus pallidus is notably effective for medically refractory DYT1 dystonia
Diagnosis is confirmed by targeted TOR1A genetic testing for the recurrent GAG deletion
reference.pathophysiology: DYT1 dystonia is caused by a recurrent in-frame trinucleotide (GAG) deletion in TOR1A, which removes a glutamic acid residue from torsinA, an ATPase of the endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear envelope. The abnormal protein disturbs nuclear envelope and endoplasmic reticulum function and impairs neuronal development and connectivity within motor circuits, particularly the basal ganglia-thalamocortical and cerebellar pathways. The result is abnormal sensorimotor integration and defective inhibition producing sustained co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles, without neurodegeneration, which is why brain structure appears normal.
additionalDifferentials: Other genetic isolated dystonias (for example THAP1-related dystonia)
Secondary dystonia from perinatal injury or structural lesions
Juvenile Huntington disease and other combined dystonia syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Targeted TOR1A genetic testing for the recurrent GAG deletion
A therapeutic levodopa trial to exclude dopa-responsive dystonia
Serum copper and caeruloplasmin (and slit-lamp examination) to exclude Wilson disease
Brain MRI, expected to be normal, to exclude structural and neurodegenerative causes
Broader dystonia gene panel where TOR1A testing is negative but the phenotype fits an isolated dystonia
redFlags: Rapid generalisation of dystonia threatening ambulation or respiration
Status dystonicus with severe, unremitting muscle contractions
Features atypical for isolated dystonia (cognitive decline, ataxia, weakness) suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Bulbar involvement compromising swallowing or airway
reference.prognosis: The dystonia is usually static or slowly progressive after an initial spreading phase and does not shorten life or cause cognitive decline; disability depends on the extent of generalisation. Many refractory cases achieve substantial, durable benefit from pallidal deep brain stimulation.
pitfalls: Omitting a levodopa trial and missing coexisting or mimicking dopa-responsive dystonia
Interpreting reduced penetrance incorrectly, for example reassuring a carrier that they cannot be affected or over-predicting risk
Attributing childhood limb dystonia to a functional cause without genetic evaluation
Delaying referral for deep brain stimulation in medically refractory generalised disease
management: Trial levodopa first to exclude and treat dopa-responsive dystonia, which can mimic it at onset
Offer oral centrally acting agents, particularly anticholinergics, which are often better tolerated in children and adolescents
Inject botulinum toxin for focal or particularly disabling body regions
Refer for pallidal deep brain stimulation in refractory, disabling generalised disease, where it gives substantial and durable benefit
Provide physiotherapy, occupational therapy and rehabilitative support
Offer genetic counselling addressing autosomal dominant TOR1A inheritance with markedly reduced penetrance, and targeted GAG-deletion testing for relatives as appropriate
Manage within a multidisciplinary neurology and movement-disorder service
